title: Pendulum before a ruler, Aachen (real footage)

narration.transcript: The string is about sixty centimetres long.

caveats: motion blur when bob moves fast through centre
tens digits of ruler numbers partly cropped but centimetre ticks are clear

reference.basis: close-up Faber-Castell wooden school ruler with centimetre and millimetre marks; assumed 30 cm long, so 1 cm spacing is 0.01 m in plane of motion

slow_motion.evidence: no caption about slow motion; observed ~1.5 s period matches ~0.6 m string in real time

stated_facts.said: The string is about sixty centimetres long.

observation.what_happens: A dark pendulum bob on a yellow string swings left-right in front of a wooden ruler. It swings continuously through the whole clip, reaching the right extreme and left extreme alternately with no release or catch visible.

calibration.note: wooden ruler = 0.3 m (close-up Faber-Castell wooden school ruler with centimetre and millimetre marks; assumed 30 cm long, so 1 cm spacing is 0.01 m in plane of motion) spans 1296 ± 5.7 px in SAM's mask (read in 3 still frames)

measured.pivotNote: a circle was fitted (centre at 368, -11468 px, radius 11862 px) but it is not a pivot: that centre lies 8.5 frame diagonals from the middle of the picture (over 1.5); no angle is measured about it; the motion is measured as the distance s along the path's straight line instead

rejectedPivot.why: the swing covers only 3° of arc; under 25° the path doesn't determine the radius (±3055 px), so L isn't measured from it
rejectedPivot.reason: that centre lies 8.5 frame diagonals from the middle of the picture (over 1.5)

given: scale: wooden ruler = 0.3 m (close-up Faber-Castell wooden school ruler with centimetre and millimetre marks; assumed 30 cm long, so 1 cm spacing is 0.01 m in plane of motion) spans 1296 ± 5.7 px in SAM's mask (read in 3 still frames), known to ±30% (its size ±30%, its length in pixels ±0.44%)
string length = 0.6 m (“The string is about sixty centimetres long.”)
pendulum length L = 0.6 m (stated): hold L fixed and measure g
reasoning: Period ~1.56 s matches 2*pi*sqrt(0.6/g) for Earth g, amplitude ~0.07 m is ~7 deg so small-angle is good but exact sine may be tested, and amplitude looks almost steady so damping is tiny. Candidates go from ideal SHO to viscous-damped SHO to exact sine with linear+quadratic air drag, all using s along the straight track with L fixed and g fitted.

critique.finding: The bob swings side to side like a tiny-angle pendulum pulling with gravity {g} around center {s_eq}. It only partly captures the motion, leaving a regular back-and-forth miss.
critique.headline: Pendulum swings steadily but ideal timing misses wobble.
critique.revision_idea: Add the finite-angle sine restoring force so the period grows with swing size. The misses swing positive-negative every cycle with high autocorrelation, exactly what a small-angle timing error leaves.
critique.why_it_won: It gets the side-to-side restoring pull right, while the falling-ball laws predict a drop that never happens.

headline: The same workshop’s 60 cm pendulum: g about 10 m/s², no error bar (the law misses the unseen swing by 21× the noise); the clock check reads real time, which is right.
finding: The bob swings side to side like a tiny-angle pendulum pulling with gravity about 10 m/s² around center about 0.009 m. It only partly captures the motion, leaving a regular back-and-forth miss.

eyeball.law_in_words: The small-angle period of a simple pendulum is T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), so with L about 0.6 m and T timed frame by frame at 25 fps, g = 4 pi^2 L / T^2, and the equilibrium plumb point is the mid-point between symmetric left and right turning points on the ruler scale.

clockCheck.why: Clock checked: gravity came out within 1.7% of Earth’s, so the clip plays in real time.

wonder.idea: Add the finite-angle sine restoring force so the period grows with swing size. The misses swing positive-negative every cycle with high autocorrelation, exactly what a small-angle timing error leaves.
